title: Freelance Irregular Income Kit
description: Pay yourself the same amount every month, even when client income is lumpy. Baseline budget, 12-month income history, step-by-step salary and buffer setup with a worked example, a month-by-month buffer planner, a lean month playbook, a 20-minute monthly routine and copy-in spreadsheet formulas. Budgeting templates, not financial advice.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Irregular Income Kit

Freelance income arrives in lumps: 7,000 one month, 1,200 the next. This kit sets up a simple system that turns uneven business income into a steady, predictable monthly pay for you, with a buffer that carries you through slow months.

It's a budgeting and planning system, not financial advice. It doesn't tell you what to invest in or how to handle your taxes; for those, speak to a qualified adviser or accountant where you live.

## The system in one paragraph

All client payments go into one **Income account**. Once a month, on the same day, you pay yourself a fixed **salary** from it into your personal account, and move your tax set-aside into a separate **Tax account**. Whatever's left stays in the Income account as a **buffer**. When a slow month comes, the buffer still pays your salary. You only raise your salary when the buffer is full.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `baseline-budget.md` | Work out your "must pay" number and your "comfortable" number |
| `income-history.csv` | Log the last 12 months of income to see your real average and your worst months |
| `pay-yourself-a-salary.md` | Set up the accounts and pick your salary, with a worked example |
| `buffer-planner.csv` | A 12-month month-by-month plan with a filled example; shows how the buffer rises and falls |
| `lean-month-playbook.md` | What to do, in order, when income drops |
| `monthly-money-routine.md` | A 20-minute routine on the same day each month |
| `spreadsheet-formulas.md` | Copy-in formulas for Excel, Google Sheets and Numbers |

## Setup (about 90 minutes, once)

1. **Baseline (30 min):** fill in `baseline-budget.md`. You'll come out with two numbers: Floor and Comfortable.
2. **History (20 min):** fill in `income-history.csv` from your bank statements or invoices. Note your average and your three lowest months.
3. **Salary (20 min):** follow `pay-yourself-a-salary.md` to choose a starting salary and buffer target.
4. **Accounts (20 min):** open or rename the accounts (Income, Tax, Personal). Most banks let you add a second account or a "pot" in minutes.

Then run `monthly-money-routine.md` once a month.

## Who this is for

- Freelancers and self-employed people with uneven monthly income
- Anyone who has had a great month and still felt broke three months later
- New freelancers building their first buffer

## A note on tax

Freelancers usually have to set money aside for income tax and social contributions, because nobody deducts it for you. The rate depends on where you live and how much you earn. This kit gives you a place to set aside a percentage; ask an accountant or your tax authority's guidance what percentage is right for you. If you don't know yet, many freelancers start by setting aside 25–30% of income received and adjust once they have proper advice.
files.baseline-budget.md:
# Baseline budget

Two numbers drive the whole system:

- **Floor:** the least you need each month to cover essentials without new debt.
- **Comfortable:** what you need to live normally, including savings and fun.

Your salary will start somewhere between the two.

Use your bank statements from the last three months. Use monthly figures: divide yearly bills by 12, and quarterly bills by 3.

## Part 1: Floor (essentials)

| Category | Monthly amount | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rent or mortgage | | |
| Utilities (energy, water) | | |
| Council / property / local taxes | | |
| Phone and internet | | |
| Groceries (basic) | | |
| Transport (basic) | | |
| Insurance (health, home, car) | | |
| Minimum debt repayments | | |
| Childcare / dependants | | |
| Medication and essential health costs | | |
| Other essentials | | |
| **Floor total** | | |

## Part 2: Comfortable (everything else)

| Category | Monthly amount | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Floor total (from above) | | |
| Groceries (normal, on top of basic) | | |
| Eating out and takeaway | | |
| Subscriptions | | |
| Clothes | | |
| Gifts and occasions | | |
| Hobbies and fun | | |
| Holidays (yearly cost ÷ 12) | | |
| Personal savings goals | | |
| Retirement contributions | | |
| Irregular costs (repairs, car service, etc. ÷ 12) | | |
| **Comfortable total** | | |

## Part 3: Business costs (don't put these in your salary)

Business costs should be paid from the Income account, not your personal salary. List them so you know how much the business needs before it can pay you.

| Cost | Monthly amount |
|---|---|
| Software and subscriptions | |
| Equipment (yearly ÷ 12) | |
| Accountant / bookkeeping | |
| Professional insurance | |
| Coworking / office | |
| Training | |
| Other | |
| **Business costs total** | |

## Your numbers

- **Floor:** [ ] per month
- **Comfortable:** [ ] per month
- **Business costs:** [ ] per month

## Worked example (fictional illustrator)

| | Monthly |
|---|---|
| Floor | 1,900 |
| Comfortable | 2,700 |
| Business costs | 180 |

So in a month, before tax set-aside, the business needs 180 for itself and wants to pay the illustrator somewhere between 1,900 and 2,700.

## Quick sanity checks

- If your Floor is more than about 70% of your average monthly income after tax and business costs, the buffer will build slowly. Look first at the biggest two lines, not the small ones.
- Irregular costs catch people out. Car repairs, annual renewals and dentist bills belong in the Comfortable budget as monthly amounts, even though you pay them occasionally.

files.pay-yourself-a-salary.md:
# Pay yourself a salary

The idea: your business gets paid irregularly; you get paid the same amount on the same day every month. The difference is absorbed by a buffer.

## Step 1: Set up three accounts

| Account | What goes in | What comes out |
|---|---|---|
| **Income** (business) | Every client payment, nothing else | Business costs, tax transfer, your salary |
| **Tax** (business or savings) | Your tax set-aside each month | Tax bills only |
| **Personal** | Your salary | Your life |

Rules:
- Clients pay into Income only. Update your invoice template if needed.
- Never spend from Tax on anything except tax.
- Never top up Personal from Income outside payday, except through the lean month playbook.

If your bank offers "pots" or sub-accounts, those work fine. Some freelancers keep Income and Tax at a different bank from Personal so the money is less tempting to dip into.

## Step 2: Find your numbers

From `baseline-budget.md` and `income-history.csv`:

- **Floor** (essentials per month)
- **Comfortable** (normal life per month)
- **Average available** (12-month average of income minus business costs minus tax set-aside)

## Step 3: Choose your starting salary

Use the lowest of these three:

1. **90% of your average available.** The 10% margin is what builds the buffer.
2. **Your Comfortable number.** No need to pay yourself more than you need while building the buffer.
3. **What your current buffer can support.** If you're starting with almost nothing, start nearer your Floor.

If that number is below your Floor, the system will still help, but the real fix is more income or lower costs. Look at `lean-month-playbook.md`, stage 3.

## Step 4: Set a buffer target

Your buffer target is how much you keep in Income after paying everything.

| Your situation | Suggested target |
|---|---|
| Steady clients, low costs, no dependants | 3 months of salary |
| Typical freelancer | 3–4 months of salary |
| Very lumpy income, big projects, or others depend on you | 6 months of salary |

## Step 5: Payday rules

On payday each month (the same date, e.g. the 1st):

1. Move your tax set-aside percentage of last month's income to Tax.
2. Pay any business costs due.
3. Pay your salary to Personal.
4. Whatever's left in Income is your buffer.

When the buffer passes your target, you have two choices:
- **Pay a bonus:** move the excess to Personal or a savings goal.
- **Raise your salary:** only if the buffer has been at or above target for three months in a row, and only by up to 10% at a time.

When the buffer is low, follow `lean-month-playbook.md`. Never cut your salary below your Floor except as a last step.

## Worked example (fictional illustrator)

From the baseline and history files:

- Floor: 1,900
- Comfortable: 2,700
- Average available: 2,205

Starting salary options:
1. 90% of 2,205 = about 1,985
2. Comfortable = 2,700
3. Starting buffer of 2,000 (one month of a 2,000 salary). That's enough to start, but not more.

Lowest is about 1,985, so the illustrator rounds to **2,000**, above the Floor of 1,900.

Buffer target: income is lumpy but there are no dependants, so **3 months = 6,000**.

See `buffer-planner.csv` for the following 12 months. In short:
- Five months fell short (December, January, April, July, August), with the biggest gap 1,355.
- The salary of 2,000 was paid every single month.
- January dropped to 860 in the buffer, which triggered stage 2 of the lean month playbook. The outreach done that month brought in February's project.
- After 12 months the buffer had grown from 2,000 to 3,480, still short of the 6,000 target, so no bonus or raise yet.

What would have happened without the system: after costs and tax, the illustrator would have had 2,520 to live on in November, 870 in December and 1,470 in January, well below the Floor of 1,900 for two months running.

## Common questions

**What if a huge payment lands?** Same rules. It goes into Income, tax is set aside, and the rest boosts the buffer. If it pushes the buffer over target, pay the excess as a bonus.

**What if a client pays late?** That's exactly what the buffer is for. Pay your salary as normal and chase the invoice.

**Should the buffer be invested?** This kit doesn't cover investing. Many people keep buffers in an easy-access account because they may need the money next month. If you want to do more, speak to a regulated adviser.

**Is a salary from my business taxed differently?** It depends on how your business is set up and where you live. For a sole trader in many countries, "paying yourself" is just moving money between your own accounts. For a limited company it may be different. Check with an accountant.

files.lean-month-playbook.md:
# Lean month playbook

Use this when your buffer drops below one month of salary (Red in `buffer-planner.csv`), or when you can see a low month coming. Work through the stages in order. Most lean spells are fixed by stages 1 and 2.

---

## Stage 1: Collect what you're owed (this week)

Money you've earned but not received is the fastest money there is.

- [ ] List every unpaid invoice, oldest first.
- [ ] Send a polite chase for anything past its due date.
- [ ] For anything due in the next 14 days, send a friendly "just confirming this is scheduled" note.
- [ ] Invoice any finished work you haven't billed yet, including small extras.
- [ ] For projects in progress, check whether a milestone payment can be invoiced now.
- [ ] For retainer clients, check next month's invoice will go out on time.

> "Hi [Name], just a quick note: invoice [number] for [amount] was due on [date]. Could you let me know when it's scheduled for payment? Thanks!"

## Stage 2: Bring in work (next 2 weeks)

- [ ] Email five past clients. Not a sales pitch; a check-in with one useful idea.
- [ ] Follow up every proposal still waiting for a reply.
- [ ] Offer existing clients a small, specific add-on with a clear price.
- [ ] Tell your network you have availability from [date].
- [ ] Revisit any "not right now" leads from the last six months.

> "Hi [Name], I was thinking about [their project / business] and had an idea: [one-line idea]. I have some space from [date] if it's useful. Happy to chat."

Spend at least an hour a day on stage 2 while you're in Red. The work you start now is often next month's income.

## Stage 3: Cut business costs (if still Red after 2 weeks)

- [ ] List every business subscription. Pause or downgrade anything you haven't used this month.
- [ ] Postpone non-urgent equipment and training purchases.
- [ ] Ask suppliers about annual-to-monthly switches or pauses.

## Stage 4: Trim personal spending (if Red for a second month)

Use your `baseline-budget.md`. Temporarily drop from Comfortable towards Floor:

- [ ] Pause savings goals and holiday saving for a month (not retirement contributions you can't restart easily, if you can avoid it).
- [ ] Cut eating out, subscriptions and non-essential shopping.
- [ ] Look for one-off income: selling unused equipment, short paid gigs.

## Stage 5: Lower your salary (last resort)

Only if the buffer is likely to run out within a month even after stages 1–4.

- [ ] Reduce salary to your Floor, not below, for one month.
- [ ] Review again next payday.
- [ ] Once the buffer is back above one month, return to your normal salary.

Never borrow from the Tax account. A shortfall there becomes a bigger, more urgent problem later.

## If things are serious

If you can't cover essentials for more than a month or two, talk to someone early: a free, independent debt or money advice service in your country, your bank, or an accountant. Problems are easier to fix before payments are missed.

---

## After the lean spell: debrief (15 minutes)

When you're back to Amber or Green, write down:

1. What caused it? (seasonal, one big client ending, late payment, a gap between projects)
2. Could you have seen it coming? When?
3. What brought the money back?
4. What will you do differently? (bigger buffer target, earlier outreach, deposit terms, more retainer work)

Common patterns worth planning for:
- **Seasonal dips** (December, August in many industries): add them to your planner in advance and start stage 2 outreach six weeks earlier.
- **One client is more than 40% of income:** if they leave, you're in Red overnight. Start building a second major client now.
- **Gaps between projects:** ask for deposits, and book the next project before the current one ends.
files.monthly-money-routine.md:
# Monthly money routine (20 minutes)

Do this on the same date each month, ideally the day before payday. Put it in your calendar as a recurring event.

## 1. Count (5 minutes)

- [ ] Add up all income received into the Income account last month.
- [ ] Add up business costs paid.
- [ ] Note any unpaid invoices and when they're due.
- [ ] Enter the month in `buffer-planner.csv`.

## 2. Pay (5 minutes)

In this order:

- [ ] Tax set-aside: [your %] of last month's income → Tax account.
- [ ] Business costs due → paid from Income.
- [ ] Salary: [your salary] → Personal account.
- [ ] If the buffer is above target: excess → bonus or savings.

## 3. Check status (2 minutes)

Closing buffer ÷ salary = months of salary in the buffer.

| Months in buffer | Status | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 3 or more | Green | Carry on. Consider a raise after 3 Green months in a row. |
| 1 to 3 | Amber | Carry on. Keep an eye on the pipeline. |
| Under 1 | Red | Start `lean-month-playbook.md`, stage 1, today. |

## 4. Look ahead (5 minutes)

- [ ] What income is confirmed for next month? (signed work, invoices due)
- [ ] What income is likely? (proposals out, retainers)
- [ ] Any big costs coming? (annual renewals, tax bills, equipment)
- [ ] Any seasonal dip in the next three months? If yes, start outreach now.

## 5. One note (3 minutes)

Write one sentence about the month. After a year you'll see your patterns clearly.

> Example: "October: two invoices paid late again, both from the same agency. Ask them for 50% upfront next time."

---

## Quarterly (an extra 15 minutes every 3 months)

- [ ] Is the Tax account on track for your next tax bill? If unsure, ask your accountant.
- [ ] Recalculate your 12-month average available in `income-history.csv`.
- [ ] Is your salary still at or below 90% of that average?
- [ ] Revisit your Floor and Comfortable numbers. Have prices or circumstances changed?
- [ ] Is any single client more than 40% of your income?

## Yearly

- [ ] Review the full year in `buffer-planner.csv`. How many Red months? What caused them?
- [ ] Adjust your buffer target if needed.
- [ ] Decide on a salary for next year.
files.spreadsheet-formulas.md:
# Spreadsheet formulas

These work in Excel, Google Sheets and Numbers. Open the CSV files, then type the formulas into the cells described. Row 1 is the header row; data starts in row 2.

## income-history.csv

Columns: A Month, B Income received, C Business costs, D Tax set-aside %, E Tax set-aside, F Available to pay yourself, G Notes.

| Cell | Formula | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| E2 | `=B2*D2/100` | Tax set-aside for the month |
| F2 | `=B2-C2-E2` | What's left to pay yourself |

Copy E2 and F2 down to row 13.

Summary (put these below your 12 months):

| What | Formula |
|---|---|
| Total income | `=SUM(B2:B13)` |
| Average income | `=AVERAGE(B2:B13)` |
| Average available | `=AVERAGE(F2:F13)` |
| Lowest month available | `=MIN(F2:F13)` |
| Average of 3 lowest months | `=AVERAGE(SMALL(F2:F13,1),SMALL(F2:F13,2),SMALL(F2:F13,3))` |
| Suggested max salary (90%) | `=ROUND(AVERAGE(F2:F13)*0.9,-1)` |

## buffer-planner.csv

Columns: A Month, B Opening buffer, C Income received, D Business costs, E Tax set-aside, F Salary paid, G Surplus or shortfall, H Bonus paid, I Closing buffer, J Months of salary in buffer, K Status, L Notes.

Put your settings in spare cells, e.g.:
- N1: `Tax %` and O1: `25`
- N2: `Salary` and O2: `2000`
- N3: `Buffer target` and O3: `6000`

| Cell | Formula | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| B2 | your starting buffer (type a number) | Month 1 opening |
| B3 | `=I2` | Each month opens with last month's close (copy down) |
| E2 | `=ROUND(C2*$O$1/100,0)` | Tax set-aside |
| F2 | `=$O$2` | Salary |
| G2 | `=C2-D2-E2-F2` | Surplus (positive) or shortfall (negative) |
| H2 | `=MAX(0,B2+G2-$O$3)` | Excess over target, paid as bonus |
| I2 | `=B2+G2-H2` | Closing buffer |
| J2 | `=ROUND(I2/F2,1)` | Months of salary in buffer |
| K2 | `=IF(J2>=3,"Green",IF(J2>=1,"Amber","Red"))` | Status |

Copy row 2 formulas down to row 13 (except B, which uses `=I2` from row 3 onwards).

## Optional: colour the Status column

- **Excel:** select column K → Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Text that Contains → "Red" → red fill. Repeat for Amber and Green.
- **Google Sheets:** select column K → Format → Conditional formatting → Text contains → "Red" → choose a colour. Add rules for Amber and Green.
- **Numbers:** select column K → Format sidebar → Cell → Conditional Highlighting → Add a Rule → Text → Contains.

## Optional: forecast with expected income

Add a column for "Confirmed" and "Likely" income for future months, then set Income received to `=Confirmed + Likely*0.5`. Counting likely work at half its value keeps the forecast realistic.
